newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: South African parties clash over casino tycoon.
newsitem.headline: South African parties clash over casino tycoon.

text.p: South Africa's ruling African National Congress on Wednesday accused the country's former rulers of having shielded casino magnate Sol Kerzner from prosecution on bribery charges.

Justice Minister Dullah Omar told the National Assembly that a 1991 bid to extradite Kerzner to the nominally independent black homeland of Transkei was stalled after his lawyers approached the then white government.

Kerzner, founder of South Africa's Sun International casino empire, was wanted in Transkei on charges of bribery, corruption and fraud linked to an alleged two million rand (then worth $2 million) hand-out to homeland leaders.
Omar said prosecutors in the region, now part of South Africa, were still investigating the case against Kerzner.
"My own attitude has been that the attorney-general should pursue the matter and exercise his discretion without fear or favour," Omar said.

ANC justice spokesman Johnny de Lange said he would ask the departments of foreign affairs and justice to explain why the former National Party (NP) government had never allowed Kerzner's case to come to court.
"They invested so much time and effort in devising methods and schemes to prevent the matter being heard in the courts.
"This shows a cover-up on a grand scale and what needs to be discovered now is why the NP...was prepared to do so, and what was received in return," de Lange said.

National Party member of parliament Sheila Camerer, rejecting the "wild allegations" of a cover-up, accused the ANC of using opportunistic propaganda tactics. "There has been no connivance," she said.
Camerer said the white cabinet had acted partly on findings by state lawyers that the extradition request was faulty on technical grounds.
National Party Secretary-General Roelf Meyer said the party had not accepted any cash from Kerzner between 1990 and April 1994 when it handed over power to the ANC.
But Kerzner, in a telephone interview with state television on Wednesday, said: "I contributed 50,000 rand to the National Party, that must have been, I would think in 1994."
Kerzner said he had also contributed half a million rand to the ANC.
